children.note: Land-policy principles, the three classes of land, non-citizen leases, land-use control, the National Land Commission and the land laws Parliament must make.

Land must be held and used fairly, productively and in a way that lasts, guided by seven listed principles. A national land policy, reviewed from time to time, and Acts of Parliament put those principles to work.

manas.q: What overall standard does Article 60 set for how land is held and used?

children.note: Every holding and use of land is measured against seven principles: fair access, secure rights, sustainable use, clean and cheap administration, care for fragile ecosystems, no gender bias, and local dispute settlement.

manas.q: Name four of the seven land-policy principles in Article 60.

children.note: Everyone should have a fair chance to get land.
A holder should not fear losing land without due process.
Land should produce without being exhausted for the next generation.
Land offices should be transparent and should not cost too much.
Wetlands, forests and similar sensitive areas are to be conserved.
Laws and customs that shut women out of land or property in land must go.
Communities are encouraged to settle land quarrels through recognised local methods, as long as they fit the Constitution.

children.topic: Clause 2: how the principles are applied
children.note: The national government drafts and regularly reviews a national land policy, and Parliament passes laws to carry the principles out.
All land belongs to the people of Kenya: the nation as a whole, its communities, and individual owners. Every piece of land falls into one of three classes: public, community or private.
Ownership rests with the people of Kenya in three ways at once: collectively as the nation, as communities, and as individuals.
Public land (Art. 62), community land (Art. 63) and private land (Art. 64). There is no fourth class.

manas.q: Into which three classes does Article 61 divide land?

children.note: Lists what counts as public land, from unalienated government land to rivers, minerals, the sea bed and national parks. Some is held by county governments and some by the national government, always in trust and managed by the National Land Commission.
Fourteen kinds, grouped below. Anything not proved to be private or community land is public by default (clause 1(m)).

manas.q: Name three kinds of public land under Article 62.

children.topic: State land and land without an owner
children.note: Former unalienated government land; land used by State organs (unless rented on a private lease); land sold or surrendered to the State; land where no owner or heir can be found.
Minerals and mineral oils; government forests, game reserves, water catchments, national parks and sanctuaries; rivers, lakes and other water bodies.
The territorial sea, exclusive economic zone, sea bed, continental shelf and the strip between high and low water marks.
Public roads under an Act; land not classed as private or community; and land an Act of Parliament declares public.

Former government land, land surrendered to the State, ownerless and heirless land, and land used by county organs belong to the county government in trust for its residents, managed by the National Land Commission.

manas.q: Who holds ownerless public land, and for whom?

children.note: Minerals, forests and parks, roads, water bodies, the sea and shore, and residual land belong to the national government in trust for all Kenyans, again managed by the National Land Commission.

children.topic: Clause 4: no disposal without an Act
children.note: Public land may only be sold, allocated or used on terms an Act of Parliament sets out. This is the constitutional answer to past "land grabbing".

manas.q: What limit does Article 62(4) put on giving away public land?

children.note: Community land belongs to communities defined by ethnicity, culture or a similar shared interest, such as group ranches, community forests, grazing land, shrines and ancestral land. It may only be dealt with under a law that sets out members' individual and shared rights.
Communities identified by ethnicity, culture or a similar common interest.

Group-registered land, land transferred to a community by law, land an Act declares community land, and land a community lawfully uses as forest, grazing or shrines, ancestral and hunter-gatherer land, and trust land held by counties.

manas.q: Give three examples of community land.

children.note: Land registered to group representatives (for example group ranches) or passed to a community by a legal process.
Community forests, grazing areas and shrines the community lawfully holds or uses.
Ancestral land and land traditionally occupied by hunter-gatherer communities.
Trust land held by county governments, except public land they hold under Article 62(2).
Until it is registered, the county government holds it in trust for the community concerned.

children.topic: Clauses 4–5: dealing with it needs a law
children.note: It cannot be sold or used except under a law setting out the rights of members one by one and together; Parliament must pass that law. Check the current Community Land Act on new.kenyalaw.org (checked 13 Nov 2026).
Private land is land held by a person on freehold or leasehold, plus any other land an Act of Parliament declares private.
Registered land owned outright with no end date.

manas.q: What two tenures make land private under Article 64?

children.note: Land held for a fixed term under a lease.
Any other land that an Act of Parliament classes as private.

A non-citizen may hold land only on lease, for at most 99 years; any document that tries to give more is read down to a 99-year lease. A company or trust counts as a citizen only if citizens own all of it.
Non-citizens cannot own freehold; their leases are capped at ninety-nine years however they were granted.

manas.q: What is the longest interest in land a non-citizen may hold?

children.topic: Clause 2: bigger grants are cut down
children.note: If a deed or agreement purports to give a non-citizen more than a 99-year lease, the law treats it as a 99-year lease and nothing more.
A company is a citizen only if wholly owned by citizens; a trust only if every beneficiary is a citizen.

manas.q: When does a company count as a citizen for landholding?

children.note: A company that is 90% Kenyan-owned and 10% foreign-owned is a non-citizen for this Article, so it can only take a lease of up to 99 years.
Parliament may pass a law to fill in how this Article works.

children.topic: Art. 66 · Regulation of land use and property
children.note: The State may control how any land or interest in land is used for defence, public safety, order, morality, health or planning. Parliament must also make sure investment in property benefits local communities and their economies.
Defence; the safety, order, morality and health of the public; and planning how land is used. Zoning rules and building controls rest on this.

manas.q: On what grounds may the State regulate land use under Article 66?

children.note: Parliament must legislate so that property investments help the communities and local economies where they happen.

Sets up the National Land Commission and gives it eight main jobs, among them managing public land for both levels of government and investigating historical land injustices. Parliament may add more functions.
The Constitution itself creates the National Land Commission (NLC), a Chapter 15 commission.
Eight functions, grouped below.

manas.q: Name three functions of the National Land Commission.

children.note: Runs public land for both the national government and the counties.
Recommends a national land policy and advises on a programme to register title across Kenya.
Researches land and natural resources and oversees land-use planning nationwide.
Investigates past and present land injustices, on its own motion or on complaint, and recommends redress.
Encourages traditional ways of settling land conflicts.
Assesses land tax and premiums on immovable property where the law designates.
National law may give the NLC further functions. Check the current National Land Commission Act on new.kenyalaw.org (checked 13 Nov 2026).

Parliament must tidy up and modernise Kenya's land laws and pass new ones on a list of topics. These include ceilings and floors on private holdings, matrimonial property and protecting widows and other dependants.
Consolidate and rationalise existing land laws, and bring sector land-use laws into line with the Article 60 principles.
Seven topics, listed below.

manas.q: Name three subjects on which Article 68 requires new land laws.

children.note: Set the smallest and largest private landholdings.
Control how land moves between public, community and private.
Recognise and protect matrimonial property, especially the home, during and after marriage.
Conserve public land, keep access to it, and review past grants of public land for legality.
Protect dependants of a deceased landholder, including a spouse living on the land.
State and personal duties to the environment, going to court for a clean environment, ratifying resource deals, and environmental laws.

children.topic: Art. 69 · Obligations in respect of the environment
children.note: The State must manage the environment and natural resources sustainably and share their benefits fairly, aiming among other things for tree cover on at least 10% of Kenya's land. Every person must also help State organs and others protect the environment.

children.topic: Clause 1: eight duties of the State
children.note: Listed below.

manas.q: What tree-cover target does Article 69 set?

children.note: Use and conserve the environment sustainably and share the benefits equitably.
Work towards, and keep, tree cover on at least a tenth of the country's land area.
Protect communities' intellectual property and traditional knowledge of biodiversity and genetic resources.
Encourage the public to take part in managing and protecting the environment.
Set up systems to assess a project's environmental impact, to audit it, and to monitor the environment.
Remove processes likely to endanger the environment, and use resources for the people's benefit.

children.topic: Clause 2: a duty on every person
children.note: Everyone must cooperate with State organs and others to conserve the environment and keep development ecologically sustainable.

manas.q: Is protecting the environment only the State's duty under Article 69?

children.note: Anyone who claims their Article 42 right to a clean, healthy environment is threatened or broken may go to court, on top of any other remedy. The applicant need not show that anyone has suffered loss or injury.
Any person who says the Article 42 right was violated, is being violated now, or probably will be; a future threat is enough.

manas.q: Under Article 70, must you wait for harm before going to court?

children.topic: Clause 2: what the court may order
children.note: Any order it thinks fit, including the three below.
Prevent or halt an act or omission that damages the environment.
Compel a public officer to take steps to stop environmental harm.
Pay compensation to a victim of the violation.

children.topic: Clause 3: no need to prove loss
children.note: The applicant does not have to show that anyone has been harmed or lost anything. This widens standing for environmental cases.

manas.q: What does Article 70(3) say an applicant need not prove?

children.topic: Art. 71 · Agreements relating to natural resources
children.note: A deal made on or after 27 August 2010 that grants anyone a right or concession to exploit Kenya's natural resources needs Parliament's ratification. Parliament must pass a law saying which classes of deal this covers.

Covers any grant of a right or concession to exploit a natural resource (for example oil, minerals, timber), whoever grants it, the national government included, if made on or after the effective date.

manas.q: Which natural-resource agreements must Parliament ratify?

children.note: Parliament defines by statute which kinds of transaction need ratification. Check which Act currently does this on new.kenyalaw.org (checked 13 Nov 2026).

children.topic: Art. 72 · Legislation relating to the environment
children.note: Parliament must pass the laws needed to give full effect to this Part on the environment and natural resources.
The main one is the Environmental Management and Co-ordination Act (EMCA), which runs NEMA and environmental impact assessment. Check the current version on new.kenyalaw.org (checked 13 Nov 2026).
